title: Competitor Map Analysis for Dealerships | GAS.net
text:
# Competitor map analysis: who shares the map with you, and why.

Competitor map analysis means looking at the dealerships and repair shops that appear in Google’s map results for your searches, and comparing their profiles with yours. Much of a Business Profile is public: its category, rating, review count, photos and hours. Set side by side, those details often show why one business appears and another does not.

Updated October 6, 2026

You do not choose your competitors on the map. Google does, one search at a time.

The dealer across town may never appear beside you, while a tire shop two blocks away shows up in every service search.

## How to think about it

1. ### Competitors change with the search.

Sales searches, service searches and parts searches each bring a different set of businesses.
2. ### They change with the location.

The three businesses shown downtown are not the three shown twenty miles out.
3. ### Most of what you need is public.

Anyone can see a profile’s category, rating, review count, photos, hours and links.
4. ### Some of it is not.

A competitor’s calls, clicks and direction requests are visible only to that profile’s owners and managers.

...

## How to run one

1. Step 1

### Pick the searches

1. Choose three to five searches that matter, across sales and service.
2. Choose three to five places in your market to search from.
3. Use a phone in each place, or a grid rank tracking tool.
2. Step 2

### Record who appears

1. Write down the three map results for each search and place.
2. Count how often each business appears.
3. Note where you appear and where you do not.
3. Step 3

### Compare profiles

1. Open the profiles that appear most often.
2. Record category, rating, review count, the date of the newest review and the newest photo.
3. Put your own profile in the same table.

## What to compare

| Item | Where to see it | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Category | On the profile, under the name | Whether they are matched to the search and you are not |
| Rating and review count | On the profile | How well known and well regarded they appear to Google |
| Newest review | Sort the reviews by newest | Whether customers are still being asked |
| Photos | The photos section | Whether the profile is being kept up |
| Department profiles | Search their name with the word service | Whether they have an entry in service searches. See service department GBP. |
| Distance from each search point | The map | How much of the result is simply location |
| Business name | On the profile | Whether words have been added against Google’s guidelines |

text:
### Relevance. Distance. Prominence.

Google documents the core local-ranking factors; Flento applies them to car dealers.

#### The documented factors

Relevance concerns the match between the business and the search. Distance depends on the searcher’s location. Prominence concerns how well known the business is, including links and reviews. Google does not sell a better local ranking or publish precise algorithm weights.

#### Build the right segment

Segment car dealers by the actual operating model, customer need and service scope. Use dealerships with comparable new or used stock and franchise model as a starting point. Record meaningful differences before treating two locations as interchangeable. Make the actual offer understandable and the business information accurate. Compare observations under consistent conditions; a larger service area or a publishing schedule does not establish a guaranteed ranking improvement.

Sources: Local ranking guidance

...

## 4. Peer comparison and measurement

### Compare businesses that answer the same need.

Flento method for defining a relevant comparison group.

#### Match the operating model

Select dealerships with comparable new or used stock and franchise model. Match geography, service mix, customer segment and fulfilment format. Record meaningful differences in availability or scope rather than ranking every business with a similar category against one undifferentiated average.

#### Record inclusion rules

Specify geography, service type, opening or contact model, language and eligible locations before collecting peer observations. Record why each dealership belongs in the set. Exclude duplicates and unrelated formats rather than adjusting the group after seeing the results.

text:
# Dealer Google Business Profile Audit

A 10-dimension, 100-point audit of a car dealership's Google Business Profile (GBP), the single highest-leverage local SEO surface for a franchise or independent dealer. The Google local pack and Google Maps drive a disproportionate share of dealer phone calls and direction requests, and a misconfigured or under-optimized GBP suppresses both even when the dealer's website is healthy.

This skill diagnoses the GBP across categories, NAP consistency, hours of operation, services and attributes, photos and visual freshness, posts and engagement, Q&A, review velocity and signal, review response discipline, and dealer-group multi-rooftop consistency.

The audit framework, dimension-by-dimension scoring, and weights are in `REFERENCE.md`. The specific tools, URLs, and verification commands per dimension are in `CHECKS.md`.

## What this audits

Ten dimensions, 100 points total:

1. **Primary category accuracy** — 12 pts
2. **Secondary categories** — 8 pts
3. **NAP consistency (Name, Address, Phone)** — 10 pts
4. **Hours of operation** — 8 pts
5. **Services list** — 10 pts
6. **Attributes** — 7 pts
7. **Photos and visual freshness** — 12 pts
8. **Posts and engagement** — 8 pts
9. **Q&A management** — 10 pts
10. **Review signal and response discipline** — 15 pts

Multi-rooftop dealer groups receive an additional overlay assessing cross-location consistency.

The skill does not audit organic web SEO (use dealer-seo-audit), AI engine citation (use dealer-aeo-audit), or technical site health (use dealer-site-score). It does pair with dealer-customer-sentiment-analyzer for deep review analysis when needed.

Verify per category from REFERENCE.md. The completeness of this list directly affects query eligibility.

In the Photos modal, scroll through "By owner" photos. Look for current model-year vehicles. Note dates if visible (some photos display upload date on hover/click).

In Photos modal, click any "By owner" photo. The date the photo was uploaded is shown. Find the most recent.

Photos modal → switch between "By owner" and "By visitors" tabs. The counts are visible.

title: Complete GBP Optimization Guide for Car Dealerships — A3 Brands
text:
## The GBP setup checklist for dealerships

Most dealers claimed their profile years ago and never went back. Here's what a properly configured dealership GBP looks like.

Primary category: get this right. Your primary category is the single strongest ranking signal for map pack visibility, according to Whitespark's 2023 Local Search Ranking Factors study. For most dealers:

- ● New and used: "New Car Dealer"
- ● Used only: "Used Car Dealer"
- ● Service-focused: "Auto Repair Shop"

Pick the one that matches your primary revenue. Don't guess. This one field affects every local search you appear in.

Secondary categories: add all that apply. Google allows up to 10 categories. Dealerships should use them. Common secondary categories:

- ● Used Car Dealer (if primary is New)
- ● Auto Repair Shop
- ● Oil Change Service
- ● Tire Shop
- ● Auto Parts Store
- ● Car Leasing Service
- ● Truck Dealer (if applicable)

Every relevant category you add expands the queries where your profile can appear.

### Service area vs. location.

Dealerships are location-based businesses. Set your address. Don't use the service area model unless you have a mobile operation. Your physical address is a core ranking factor for proximity-based searches.

### Business description.

You get 750 characters. Use them. Include your OEM brands, your city, your primary services (sales, service, parts), and what makes you different. Don't keyword stuff, write it for a buyer scanning your profile in 10 seconds.

### Hours.

Set separate hours for each department. Sales hours. Service hours. Parts hours. Wrong hours are one of the top reasons buyers leave negative reviews. Google also uses hours data to determine when to show your profile in results.

Primary Category Selection Guide

| Dealership Type | Primary Category | Key Secondary Categories |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New & Used Sales | New Car Dealer | Used Car Dealer, Auto Repair Shop, Car Leasing |
| Used Only | Used Car Dealer | Auto Repair Shop, Car Leasing Service |
| Service-Focused | Auto Repair Shop | Oil Change Service, Tire Shop, Auto Parts |
| Truck / Commercial | Truck Dealer | New Car Dealer, Auto Repair Shop, Auto Parts |

...

## Photos and videos that actually help rankings

Google has confirmed that businesses with photos receive 42% more requests for directions and 35% more click-throughs to websites compared to those without (Google, 2024). For dealerships, photos do two things: they signal to Google that your profile is active, and they signal to buyers that your store is real.

### What to upload:

- ● Exterior shots. Front of dealership. Signage clearly visible. Multiple angles. This is what buyers look for when driving to your store.
- ● Interior shots. Showroom floor. Waiting area. Finance office. Buyers want to know what they're walking into.
- ● Team photos. Sales team. Service advisors. Your GM. Real people make the profile feel human. Stock photos do the opposite.
- ● Inventory highlights. New arrivals. Featured models. Special editions. This isn't about selling a specific car, it's about showing Google and buyers that your lot is stocked and active.
- ● Service bays. Lifts, equipment, clean shop floor. Fixed ops searches are high-intent and high-margin. Show the facility.

### Frequency matters.

Upload at least 5 new photos per week. Google tracks upload frequency as an engagement signal. A profile that gets new photos weekly signals an active, operating business. A profile with no uploads in 6 months looks abandoned, because from Google's perspective, it might be.

### Videos work too.

Short walkarounds of new inventory. Service department tours. Quick GM introductions. Keep them under 30 seconds. Google Business Profile supports video uploads directly.

### One rule: no stock photography.

Buyers spot it instantly. Google's image recognition can identify generic stock images. Use real photos of your real store.

Quick Win: Photo Upload Schedule

Assign one person at your dealership to take 5 photos every Monday morning. New arrivals on the lot, a shot of the service drive, a team photo. Upload them to GBP before lunch. This single habit — 15 minutes per week — keeps your profile permanently active in Google's eyes.

...

If someone posts an incorrect or malicious answer, flag it for removal through GBP. Google typically removes clearly false content within a few days.

## Attributes and services checklist

Google gives you two tools most dealers ignore: attributes and services. Both expand the searches where your profile appears.

Attributes are binary markers, yes/no signals about your business. Google uses them to filter search results. When a buyer searches "wheelchair accessible dealership" or "dealership with Wi-Fi," Google checks attributes.

Mark every applicable attribute:

- ● Wheelchair accessible
- ● Wi-Fi available
- ● Restroom available
- ● LGBTQ+ friendly
- ● Women-led (if applicable)
- ● Veteran-led (if applicable)
- ● Identifies as Black-owned / Latino-owned (if applicable)
- ● Appointment required / Walk-ins welcome
- ● Online estimates available

Every checked attribute is a potential search filter match.

Services let you list specific offerings. For dealerships, this means listing every service your shop performs:

- ● Oil change (conventional and synthetic)
- ● Tire rotation
- ● Tire balancing
- ● Wheel alignment
- ● Brake inspection and repair
- ● Battery testing and replacement
- ● State inspection
- ● Emissions testing
- ● Transmission service
- ● Coolant flush
- ● Air conditioning service
- ● Recall repairs
- ● Factory-scheduled maintenance
- ● Detailing

List all of them. Each service you add is a keyword signal to Google. When someone searches "tire rotation near me," Google checks which businesses in the area have "tire rotation" listed as a service. If you didn't add it, you're not in the running.

This takes 15 minutes to complete. Most dealers never do it.

15 min

Adding all applicable attributes and services to your GBP takes about 15 minutes. Each service you add is a keyword signal that expands the searches where your profile appears. Most dealers never do it.

title: Automotive SEO in 2026: What Still Works, From 69 Dealers
text:
## Key takeaways

- Organic search is still the biggest channel a dealership has, at 24% of website sessions, ahead of direct, paid search and Performance Max.
- Blog, how-to and guide pages kept only 45% of last year's clicks; homepages kept 91% and inventory pages 80%. Informational pages were 73% of every click lost.
- The how-to pages did not lose rankings. Their click-through rate fell from 2.1% to 1.4% because the AI Overview answers above them. Branded, commercial and local click-through rates all rose.
-

...

## Reviews benchmark: the local signal that moves organic too

Reviews are 20% of what decides the Google Maps pack, an all-time high in the 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey. What surprised me in our own data is how closely they track the website’s organic clicks. Across 77 dealership locations, the correlation between a store’s Google Business Profile actions and its organic website clicks is 0.73, and between its review count and organic clicks it is 0.61. That is a stronger relationship than domain rating has.

Review count is also the single best predictor of profile actions we found. Across 122 dealership locations over the past year, the median store with fewer than 100 Google reviews got 23 phone calls a month from its profile. With 500 to 1,499 reviews, 344. With 1,500 or more, 639. Part of that is size, since big stores collect big review counts, but when we controlled for it in an earlier cut the stores past 1,000 reviews still took about seven times the calls. Rating, past a point, does not matter at all: the median rating is 4.6 in every bucket. Fresh reviews matter more than the star, and specific reviews matter more than either, because AI answers now quote them.

Median monthly phone calls from Google Business Profile, by review count

23

68

344

639

Under 100 reviews 100 to 499 500 to 1,499 1,500 and up

Google Business Profile phone calls per month, median location in each band, September 2025 to August 2026. Review counts from the Business Profile API. Hover a bar for the number of locations and the median rating.

One more finding from the same profiles: over the past year, calls from the profile fell 10% and website clicks fell 9%, while direction requests rose 6%. The shopper who used to call is increasingly just driving over. Directions are the action to optimize for. Ask for “mention the Grand Highlander and that Sam made it a no-pressure process,” not “please leave five stars.”

...

## The automotive SEO plan for 2026, ranked by what the data supports

1. Stop feeding the how-to blog. It is 92% of the decline and none of the growth. Refresh your best three service how-tos and freeze the rest.
2. Build numbered buying guides and vehicle attribute pages. Ten deep, data-backed pages a month beat fifteen thin ones. Lead with the answer in the first sentence, add a spec table, real photos and an FAQ with structured data, and link every page into a hub. A page without images is unfinished.
3. Publish numbers nobody else has. Real lease payments, money factors dated to the month, your state’s lease tax mechanics, the trims your market actually buys. This is the most citable content a dealership can create.
4. Give every service its own page. A dedicated page per service was the second-ranked AI visibility factor in the 2026 survey, ahead of reviews and links. Brake service, tires, express lane, collision, fleet. Not one “Service” page.
5. Run reviews like a campaign. Get past 1,000 on Google, keep 100 or more coming a quarter, reply to most of them, and ask for specifics. Rotate a share of requests to DealerRater, Cars.com and Edmunds.
6. Fix crawlability and structured data. Server-rendered vehicle data, AutoDealer and vehicle schema, FAQ markup, a clean Merchant Center feed, and open robots.txt for the AI crawlers.
7. Escape single-digit domain rating, then stop chasing it. Twenty hours a month of local, relevant links. Never buy them.
8. Judge it by Search Console and leads, not GA4 organic. Analytics files a growing share of search and AI visits under Direct. Impressions up with clicks flat is now the signature of AI visibility, not a problem.

title: GBP for Car Dealerships and Auto Services
text:
## Showroom and service centre are two different listings

Google allows a separate listing for a department that genuinely operates as one: its own customer-facing entrance, staff, phone number, hours and a different primary category. Sales and aftersales usually meet all five. The service desk is often round the side of the building, opens at 07:30 for drop-off while the showroom opens at 09:00, and has a direct line that bypasses the sales switchboard.

Splitting them matters because the queries do not overlap. A combined listing sitting under a car dealer category will not compete properly for MOT, servicing or clutch replacement searches, which are high-volume, high-intent and repeat. Separate the service listing and it competes with the independent garages, which is the fight you actually want. The same test applies to the bodyshop and to a used-car satellite pitch.

Important

Do not split a department that shares one desk, one phone and one set of hours. That is a duplicate listing, and duplicates in automotive get merged, suppressed or suspended. The recovery process is slower than the ranking gain you were chasing.

...

## Make and model in categories and services

Google's category list is unusually granular for automotive. Franchised dealers should check whether a brand-specific dealer category exists for their marque and use it as the primary, because that is the phrasing customers search. Independents selling several marques belong under used car dealer. On the aftersales side the useful primaries are auto repair shop, MOT testing station, auto body shop and tyre shop.

The services section is where make and model detail belongs, and it is the most underused field on a dealer profile. List the actual jobs, phrased the way customers ask for them:

- Routine work - MOT test, interim and full service, brake pads and discs, wheel alignment, air conditioning regas
- Bigger jobs - cambelt replacement, clutch replacement, DPF cleaning, gearbox work, fault diagnostics
- Newer demand - EV battery health check, hybrid servicing, ADAS calibration after a windscreen change

Each service takes a short description, and that is where the marques go: which makes you are approved to work on and which you can code and program. What you must not do is cram makes into the business name. The name must match the signage, and "Anytown Motors Ford Vauxhall BMW Servicing MOT" is a violation competitors report quickly.

Worth doing

Read your competitors' review text, not just their listing. If a third of a nearby garage's reviews mention hybrid batteries or commercial vans, there is a service line with local demand you are probably qualified for and not listing.

## Photos that sell a forecourt

Car buyers look at pictures for longer than in almost any other local category, and they want specific reassurance: does this place look like it will still exist in three years. The set that earns its place:

- Wide forecourt shot - stock visible, decent light, ideally on a day the pitch is full
- The approach - the frontage from both directions of travel, because most dealerships sit on roads where you get one chance to spot the entrance
- Workshop - ramps in use, technicians working, diagnostic equipment. This is what convinces somebody to trust you with a cambelt
- Service reception - people booking a full day's work want to know where they will be sitting

Two practical rules. Blur or crop customer plates and faces. And do not upload manufacturer press pack images: they are the same files the dealer twelve miles away uploaded, and they tell a buyer nothing about your site.
